story.name: Story Makers
story.summary: Make characters move, talk and tell your own stories. Picture blocks; no other app needed.

game.name: Game Makers
game.summary: Build games with scores, choices and challenges. Start here, then explore Scratch.

dev.name: Game Developers
dev.ages: Suggested ages 11+ · or ready for typed code
dev.summary: Practice code, build in Godot and play your game on a computer or Retroid.

lessons.title: Meet your companion
lessons.concept: A command tells your character what to do. Run follows your commands.
steps: Add Move right with a value of 1
lessons.recall: What changed when you pressed Run?
lessons.hint: Press a command in the toolbox to add it.
lessons.challenge: Try another theme without changing your commands.

lessons.title: A bigger step
lessons.concept: A number changes how far the same command moves a character.
lessons.hint: The number box inside a block is editable.
lessons.challenge: Find a number that stops near the middle.

lessons.title: First, then next
lessons.concept: A sequence runs in order, from top to bottom.
lessons.hint: Use the up and down buttons to change block order.

lessons.title: Up and down
lessons.concept: Characters have a position. Up and down change one part of it.
steps: Run and find the finishing spot
lessons.recall: Did the character finish higher or lower?
lessons.hint: One down step cancels one up step.

lessons.title: Change the order
lessons.concept: The same commands can tell a different story in a new order.
steps: Swap the blocks and run both versions
lessons.recall: How did the order change the story?
lessons.hint: Use the block's earlier/later controls.

lessons.title: Take a breath
lessons.concept: Wait pauses a sequence before the next action.
lessons.hint: Wait uses seconds, not movement steps.
lessons.challenge: Use two pauses in a conversation.

lessons.title: Show what you know
lessons.concept: You can create a sequence without copying someone else's.
steps: Make move, say and wait actions
lessons.recall: Which command would you change first?
lessons.hint: A tiny finished story is enough.

lessons.title: Do it again
lessons.concept: Repeat performs the same movement several times.
steps: Compare with three Move right 1 blocks
lessons.recall: What does the repeat count mean?
lessons.hint: Repeat has a direction, step size and count.

lessons.title: Count the repeats
lessons.concept: Changing a loop count changes how many times it acts.
lessons.hint: Count the repetitions on your fingers.

lessons.title: Say it your way
lessons.concept: Speech gives a character personality; your words are part of the program.
steps: Add a short greeting in Say
Change the greeting to fit your theme
lessons.recall: What stayed the same when words changed?
lessons.hint: Short phrases fit on the stage.
lessons.challenge: Tell a joke in two speech blocks.

lessons.title: Two companions
lessons.concept: A program can choose which character receives its actions.
lessons.recall: Which character did each block control?
lessons.hint: The companion number is on each block.

lessons.title: When I tap
lessons.concept: An event starts a program when something happens.
steps: Change the trigger to Tap character
Tap your character to start the sequence
lessons.hint: Run prepares tap-triggered programs; then tap the stage character.
lessons.challenge: Give the character a surprise greeting.

lessons.title: A little tune
lessons.concept: Sound can give feedback when an action happens.
steps: Run, then try the sound-off switch
lessons.recall: Can the story work without sound?
lessons.hint: A tap or Run unlocks sound on most browsers.
lessons.challenge: Pair a tune with a movement.

lessons.title: Fix the mix-up
lessons.concept: Debugging means finding why the result differs from your plan.
steps: Reorder the blocks and run again
lessons.hint: Change one thing at a time.
lessons.challenge: Ask a sibling to mix up two blocks.

lessons.title: A new scene
lessons.concept: A scene is a new part of your story. You can create two scenes.
steps: Choose Scene 2 and a background theme
lessons.hint: Each scene has its own program and starting layout.
lessons.challenge: Use a different companion in Scene 2.

lessons.title: Go to the next scene
lessons.concept: A scene-change command moves the story to another page.
steps: In Scene 1 add a short greeting
lessons.hint: Next scene starts the other scene's Start program.

lessons.title: Send a message
lessons.concept: A message lets one sequence start another character's sequence.
lessons.recall: What made the other scene start?
lessons.hint: Send message uses the Message trigger in the other scene.

lessons.title: Hide and reveal
lessons.concept: Showing and hiding a character can create a surprise.
lessons.recall: What was hidden during the wait?
lessons.hint: Hidden characters still have their own position.
lessons.challenge: Add a greeting after the reveal.

lessons.title: Choose a beginning
lessons.concept: A story needs a clear way to start.
steps: Use a Start trigger in Scene 1
lessons.recall: Would a friend know how to begin?
lessons.hint: The stage title and Run button help the player.
lessons.challenge: Try a Tap character beginning instead.

lessons.title: Choose your story
lessons.concept: A small plan helps you finish something that is your own.
steps: Write or say a beginning and ending
lessons.hint: Choose one idea you can finish.
lessons.challenge: Use two scenes if you want.

lessons.title: Build the beginning
lessons.concept: The first scene introduces the character and goal.
lessons.hint: You can keep the program short.

lessons.title: Build the middle
lessons.concept: The middle shows something happening or changing.
lessons.hint: A pause can make a moment clearer.

lessons.title: Build the ending
lessons.concept: An ending tells the player that the story is finished.
lessons.recall: How will the player know it ended?
lessons.hint: Say The end is a good first ending.

lessons.title: Make it tappable
lessons.concept: A tap event lets the player take part.
steps: Choose Tap character for a scene
Reset, Run and test the tap
lessons.hint: Tell your player which character to tap.

lessons.title: Make it readable
lessons.concept: Clear words and actions help someone understand your creation.
lessons.recall: What helped you understand the story?
lessons.hint: Say one thing at a time.

lessons.title: Catch-up and play
lessons.concept: Rest and revision are part of learning. Choose one unfinished task.
lessons.recall: What would you like to improve?
lessons.hint: You do not have to add a new feature today.

lessons.title: Test with a friend
lessons.concept: A playtest reveals what a new player finds confusing.
lessons.recall: Where did your player need help?
lessons.hint: Observe before changing the program.

lessons.title: Fix one thing
lessons.concept: Small fixes can make a story easier to enjoy.
lessons.hint: Save a backup before a large change.
lessons.challenge: Explain the fix in your own words.

lessons.title: Save your creation
lessons.concept: A saved project lets you return and make another version.
steps: Save or download its project file
Reset and replay to verify it
lessons.recall: Where will you find your creation later?
lessons.hint: Guests can keep a local draft on their own device or download it.

lessons.title: Creator showcase
lessons.concept: You can explain and improve a program you made.
steps: Explain an event and a repeat
Change one command without a recipe
lessons.recall: Which part did you make yourself?
lessons.hint: A short story you understand is a success.
lessons.challenge: Plan a new story for November.

lessons.title: Meet the game lab
lessons.concept: Games follow rules written as commands.
lessons.hint: The browser lab is a small teaching tool.

lessons.title: Positions on the stage
lessons.concept: Position is described by horizontal and vertical movement.
lessons.hint: Up and down change the vertical position.

lessons.title: Events start actions
lessons.concept: An event is a reason for a program to run.
lessons.hint: Run arms a tap-triggered program.
lessons.challenge: Create a welcome after a tap.

lessons.title: Variables remember
lessons.concept: A variable stores a value that can change.
steps: Place three treasures on the stage
Run and check the score display
lessons.hint: Tap the stage in Layout mode to place treasures.

lessons.title: Collect a treasure
lessons.concept: Contact with a treasure can increase the score.
steps: Place one treasure near the player
lessons.hint: Collectibles are gathered when the character gets close.
lessons.challenge: Collect two treasures with one route.

lessons.title: Conditions choose
lessons.concept: An if-condition performs an action only when its test is true.
steps: Add If score reached target, say You win
lessons.hint: Set a small target while testing.

lessons.title: Build without a recipe
lessons.concept: A small independent build checks what you understand.
lessons.recall: What part could you change alone?
lessons.hint: Reuse ideas, but choose your own route.
lessons.challenge: Ask someone to predict the score.

lessons.title: Loops save repetition
lessons.concept: A repeat block replaces identical actions.
steps: Replace them with Repeat right count 3
lessons.hint: Repeat count means total repetitions.
lessons.challenge: Use a loop to collect a row.

lessons.title: Tune the speed
lessons.concept: A speed value changes how fast movement happens.
lessons.hint: Speed changes timing, not the number of steps.

lessons.title: Tap controls
lessons.concept: A game needs controls its players can use.
lessons.recall: Can you play without a keyboard?
lessons.hint: The arrow keys also work in Controls mode.
lessons.challenge: Test on a tablet in landscape.

lessons.title: A fair obstacle
lessons.concept: A hazard introduces a consequence; feedback tells players what happened.
steps: In Layout mode place a hazard
Move it to a fairer spot
lessons.hint: Reset clears the current play state.

lessons.title: An ending and replay
lessons.concept: A game should tell players when they win and let them play again.
lessons.hint: Score and collected items reset; your layout stays.

lessons.title: Your own small game
lessons.concept: Design combines a player, action, goal and challenge.
lessons.hint: Keep the first game tiny.
lessons.challenge: Try another theme with the same rules.

lessons.title: Test your rules
lessons.concept: Testing includes trying things that should fail.
steps: Try a route that misses a treasure
lessons.hint: Write down one issue to fix.

lessons.title: Meet Scratch
lessons.concept: Scratch lets you build larger projects with sprites and blocks.
steps: Open Scratch Create on a compatible computer
Find stage, sprites and code area
Save a project on the computer
lessons.recall: Which part is like our stage?
lessons.hint: Use the Scratch guide in Help; no public sharing is required.
lessons.challenge: Give your sprite a themed name.

lessons.title: Move a Scratch sprite
lessons.concept: Events and motion blocks become a playable character.
steps: Add when right arrow pressed, change x by 10
lessons.hint: Start with one direction, then add others.
lessons.challenge: Add an on-screen button for touch.

lessons.title: Scratch repetition
lessons.concept: A forever loop checks rules while a game runs.
steps: Add a forever block under the green flag
Inside use if key right arrow pressed
lessons.hint: Keep the if block inside forever.

lessons.title: Scratch treasure
lessons.concept: A second sprite can detect contact with the player.
steps: Under green flag use forever and if touching Player
lessons.hint: Choose your actual player name in touching.
lessons.challenge: Make it appear at a random position.

lessons.title: Scratch score
lessons.concept: A variable counts the treasures collected.
steps: Change score by 1 before hiding a touched treasure
lessons.hint: Avoid adding score repeatedly for one contact.
lessons.challenge: Show the score on the stage.

lessons.title: Plan the finished game
lessons.concept: A one-page plan keeps the game manageable.
steps: Write player, action, goal and hazard
lessons.hint: A five-treasure collector is enough.

lessons.title: Build the player
lessons.concept: Complete the controls before adding more features.
lessons.hint: Keep movement code on the player sprite.

lessons.title: Build collectibles
lessons.concept: Several treasures make the goal interesting.
lessons.hint: Use show at the start and hide after collection.
lessons.challenge: Use clones if you already understand them.

lessons.title: Build the hazard
lessons.concept: A hazard needs a clear consequence.
steps: Send a Lose broadcast or stop the round
lessons.hint: A separate lose message helps coordinate sprites.

lessons.title: Win and restart
lessons.concept: Broadcasts can coordinate a complete ending.
steps: When score reaches target broadcast Win
Show a win backdrop or message
Reset score and show treasures on green flag
lessons.hint: Test replay, not just the first win.

lessons.title: Explain the controls
lessons.concept: Good instructions help players start independently.
steps: Ask a sibling to start without help
lessons.hint: Use large touch targets if needed.

lessons.title: Catch-up day
lessons.concept: Finishing matters more than adding features.
lessons.hint: Remove a feature if it prevents finishing.
lessons.challenge: Play someone else's creation with permission.

lessons.title: Family playtest
lessons.concept: Feedback helps you find confusing rules.
lessons.hint: Ask where they got stuck.

lessons.title: Fix and balance
lessons.concept: Make one change and retest before making another.
lessons.hint: Keep a saved copy before editing.

lessons.title: Save the source
lessons.concept: A project file preserves the editable game.
steps: Use File > Save to your computer
Reopen it to check it works
lessons.recall: Is a screenshot an editable project?
lessons.hint: The project file, not the picture, contains the blocks.

lessons.title: Game night
lessons.concept: A finished game is playable and explainable.
steps: Explain a variable, loop and condition
lessons.recall: What are you proud of learning?
lessons.hint: Browser-lab projects count as browser creations; Scratch projects are tracked separately.

lessons.title: Your first instructions
lessons.concept: A program is a precise sequence. Our lab uses teaching commands, not GDScript.
steps: Change the number and run again
lessons.hint: The lab command list is beside the editor.

lessons.title: Variables and values
lessons.concept: Values control behavior; real variables give values names.
steps: Read the GDScript variable example in the guide
lessons.recall: What can you change without rewriting the rule?
lessons.hint: Our small lab has speed and target commands.

lessons.title: Functions are reusable actions
lessons.concept: A function gives a reusable action a name.
steps: Read the function example and identify the function body
lessons.recall: Why put an action in a function?
lessons.hint: Indentation groups GDScript statements.
lessons.challenge: Describe a function in everyday language.

lessons.title: If makes a decision
lessons.concept: Conditions decide whether an action should run.
steps: Run a route with and without a pickup
lessons.hint: The lab uses ifwin as a limited teaching command.

lessons.title: Loops repeat work
lessons.concept: Loops perform actions several times.
steps: Find the loop in the GDScript example
lessons.recall: When would a loop simplify code?
lessons.hint: The lab repeat syntax is repeat COUNT DIRECTION STEPS.

lessons.title: Debug a program
lessons.concept: Useful debugging compares expected behavior with actual behavior.
lessons.recall: What did the error tell you?
lessons.hint: This lab rejects unknown commands rather than executing arbitrary code.
lessons.challenge: Change one thing at a time.

lessons.title: Independent browser challenge
lessons.concept: Understanding means predicting, changing and explaining.
lessons.recall: Which part can you explain without help?
lessons.hint: You may use the command reference, but choose your own route.

lessons.title: Meet Godot
lessons.concept: Nodes do jobs; scenes group nodes into reusable pieces.
steps: Install the current stable Godot 4 standard edition
Create a Node2D main scene and save it
lessons.hint: Help includes setup steps and official documentation.

lessons.title: Player scene
lessons.concept: CharacterBody2D provides a useful starting point for controlled movement.
steps: Add Sprite2D or Polygon2D and CollisionShape2D
Save Player.tscn and instance it in Main
lessons.recall: Which node holds the collision shape?
lessons.hint: Use a simple shape before detailed art.

lessons.title: Move and test early
lessons.concept: Input actions separate controls from game logic.
steps: Add movement actions in Project Settings > Input Map
Attach the movement script from Help
Run on the computer and test one controller if available
lessons.recall: Why use actions instead of a specific key everywhere?
lessons.hint: Check script node type and exact action names.
lessons.challenge: Parent can start Android export setup now.

lessons.title: A pickup area
lessons.concept: Area2D signals tell us when another body enters an area.
steps: Create a treasure Area2D with art and CollisionShape2D
Remove the treasure when the player enters
lessons.recall: Why use an area for a pickup?
lessons.hint: Check collision layers and masks if it does not fire.
lessons.challenge: Print a message before adding score.

lessons.title: Score and signals
lessons.concept: Signals let objects report events without owning all game logic.
steps: Give the treasure a collected signal
Increment score in Main and update a Label
lessons.hint: The pickup guide shows a minimal signal pattern.
lessons.challenge: Keep the player separate from the score label.

lessons.title: Reusable scenes
lessons.concept: One scene can create many instances of the same object.
lessons.recall: What changes in every instance when you edit the scene?
lessons.hint: Use a scene instance, not five copied scripts.

lessons.title: Checkpoint and backup
lessons.concept: A working checkpoint makes experiments safer.
steps: Copy the folder or commit it to your own version control
lessons.hint: Do not back up only the exported APK.
lessons.challenge: Write one problem to solve next.

lessons.title: A hazard
lessons.concept: Hazards need detection and a clear consequence.
steps: Tell Main to switch to a losing state
lessons.recall: How does the player learn what happened?
lessons.hint: Start with a stationary hazard.
lessons.challenge: Add a brief visual feedback effect.

lessons.title: Game states
lessons.concept: Playing, won and lost should allow different actions.
steps: Add a state variable or enum in Main
Show distinct win and lose messages
lessons.recall: What should be disabled after a loss?
lessons.hint: A single owner for state avoids conflicting rules.
lessons.challenge: Pause the player after an ending.

lessons.title: Timer and victory
lessons.concept: A Timer can introduce a time limit without manual counting.
steps: Connect timeout to the losing state
Stop the timer after collecting the target
lessons.recall: Which event ends the round first?
lessons.hint: Test with a generous time limit first.

lessons.title: Restart and handheld test
lessons.concept: Restart must restore all state, objects and controls.
steps: Reload the current scene or reset all state
Parent exports an early APK and tests on Retroid
lessons.hint: Android setup guide lists tools and export steps.
lessons.challenge: Record controller button names on the device.

lessons.title: Art and sound
lessons.concept: Feedback supports understanding rather than hiding the rules.
steps: Add one pickup sound and a visible score change
lessons.recall: Can the player still understand the result?
lessons.hint: Use properly licensed or original assets.

lessons.title: Design your own collector
lessons.concept: Scope keeps an original project finishable.
steps: Write player, action, goal and hazard
lessons.recall: What is the smallest complete version?
lessons.hint: Keep one level and one main action.

lessons.title: Build the core
lessons.concept: Build the playable action before polish.
steps: Start your own project or adapt your checkpoint
lessons.hint: Use what you already understand.
lessons.challenge: Explain your script without reading it verbatim.

lessons.title: Build the level
lessons.concept: A level arranges reusable rules in space.
lessons.recall: Can the player reach every item?
lessons.hint: Avoid unreachable corners.
lessons.challenge: Use an array to organize objects.

lessons.title: Add a fair challenge
lessons.concept: Difficulty should come from understandable rules.
steps: Tune player speed and hit areas
lessons.hint: Ask a new player before adding more hazards.
lessons.challenge: Add one moving hazard if time allows.

lessons.title: Finish the round
lessons.concept: Win, lose and replay turn a prototype into a game.
lessons.hint: Many bugs appear only after restart.

lessons.title: Controller-friendly UI
lessons.concept: A handheld game must be usable without a mouse.
steps: Test navigating and starting with the controller
lessons.recall: Where did you still need a mouse?
lessons.hint: Use ui_accept and focus neighbors for buttons.

lessons.title: Catch-up and scope cut
lessons.concept: Removing unfinished extras can save a release.
steps: Remove an optional feature that is still broken
lessons.hint: One polished level is enough.

lessons.title: Playtest on real hardware
lessons.concept: Computer success does not guarantee handheld usability.
steps: Run on Retroid with a parent
Record controls, text readability and performance
lessons.hint: Observe a new player without coaching.

lessons.title: Fix the biggest bugs
lessons.concept: Prioritize crashes and broken rules before decoration.
steps: Check another player can start alone
lessons.hint: Keep a known-good backup.

lessons.title: Release checklist
lessons.concept: Source files and exports serve different purposes.
steps: Save and back up the source project
Export a working APK for the Retroid test device
lessons.recall: Which file lets you edit the game later?
lessons.hint: The APK plays; the Godot project edits.

lessons.title: Developer showcase
lessons.concept: Ownership means understanding the game and its code.
steps: Explain a function, signal and state
Make one independent change and rebuild
lessons.recall: What can you build next without AI writing it?
lessons.hint: A reference guide is allowed; explain your own decisions.
